title: Rebuilding Credit After Collections
subtitle: Build a recovery file before you build another credit application

blocks.text: A collection notice has the manners of a parking ticket and the staying power of a smoke alarm that wants a new battery.
Panic, shame and a midnight credit-card application will not help. A file will.

This course shows you how to check what a collector is claiming and spot what is wrong. You will keep a record of every contact, pick a way to settle that you can keep, and build new on-time history. A paid collection can still show on your reports for a while, so you cannot erase it. What you can do is build better proof of how you handle credit now.
A collection entry is a fact about one account. It is not a character reference, a personality test or a forecast for life.

items.text: True information can stay on your report for the normal reporting period, even after you pay. Paying can change the status. It does not promise the entry will be deleted.

sections.title: The File That Finally Made the Phone Stop Running the Meeting

blocks.text: Meet Ariane
paragraphs: Ariane LeBlanc runs the lunch crew at a catering company in Moncton. She has found the perfect apartment. Then the landlord frowns at a page: “There’s a collection on your file. An old mobile account.”
Two days later, mid-lunch rush, a collector calls. He wants the full balance today. Her thumb hovers over the pay link.
She grabs a pen instead. Name, company, number, original creditor, amount. “I’ll answer after I check my records,” she says.
That night she lines up her final phone bill, bank statements and both credit reports. The account is hers, but the balance includes a phone she sent back. The courier receipt proves it.

She sends a written dispute with copies, never originals. The company drops the phone charge. The rest is real, so she sets up a two-payday plan in writing and keeps every receipt. When one bureau still shows the old balance, she disputes that too.
The collection did not vanish. Credit reporting has never been famous for dramatic exits. But her file was accurate, the debt was done and her new habits were on the record.
The next time an unknown number rang during the lunch rush, Ariane did not flinch. She had a folder for that.

blocks.text: The best reply to a collector starts with proof. Check the account before you discuss payment, so a mistake does not become an expensive guess.
What changed the outcome?

Ariane slowed the whole thing down. She proved the part that was wrong, settled the part that was right and kept every paper. There was no miracle jump in her score. There was control, accurate records and a recent pattern that the next landlord or lender could read.
A simple six-item file makes your next collector call short, calm and on your terms.
blocks.detail: You will know what to check before any money moves, so a rushed payment never replaces a documented one.
blocks.extra: Next, the Verify section shows exactly what goes in the file.

sections.title: Verify Before You Volunteer a Dollar

blocks.text: When a collector reaches out, treat the first talk as fact-finding.
You do not need to decide anything while someone waits on the line.
Put these six items in the file

items.title: Collector identity
items.text: Write down the agency, the caller’s name, how to reach them and any licence number on the written notice.

items.title: Debt identity
items.text: Write down who the money was first owed to, the account reference, the balance and how fees or interest are counted.

items.title: Your records
items.text: Gather statements, receipts, cancellation emails, letters and proof of past payments. Keep the originals.

items.title: Credit evidence
items.text: Get your current reports from both Equifax and TransUnion. They may not match.

items.title: Contact log
items.text: For every call or letter, note the date, the time, who spoke, what they promised and what happens next.

items.title: Province checkpoint
items.text: Note which province or territory you live in, and which consumer office oversees collectors there.

blocks.text: The collector, the original creditor and the credit bureau each have a different job. A fix may need contact with more than one of them.
A CALM CALLBACK SCRIPT

“I’m checking the account. Please send me the original creditor, the amount with a breakdown, your agency details and a written notice. I’ll reply after I compare it with my records. I’m not agreeing to any payment on this call.”

Never share passwords, PINs or full copies of your ID just because a caller asks. Use contact details you have verified yourself. If the account is not yours, the balance is wrong, you already paid it or the dates are off, collect your proof and use the bureau and creditor dispute steps.

items.title: “Collectors in Canada all follow one national rulebook.”
items.text: Most rules for collection agencies are set by the province or territory. Federal rules also apply in some cases, such as when a federally regulated bank is collecting.

sections.title: Resolve the Valid Debt Without Buying a Promise

blocks.text: Once you have checked the account and the amount, compare your options with your cash flow. A plan that makes you miss rent or utilities, or sends you to a high-interest loan, only moves the emergency to a different envelope.
Paying in full, settling and a payment plan are three different cash-flow paths. None of them gives you a right to have true history deleted.
Before money moves

items.title: Get the deal in writing, and check the payment details yourself before you send money.
Keep proof of every payment, the settlement letter, receipts and a note of the final status.
Do not count on a spoken promise that an entry will be deleted or that your score will jump by a set number.
For an older debt, check your province’s limitation law before you pay or sign anything that admits you owe it. The limitation clock and the credit-reporting clock are two different things.
“If the limitation period has passed, the debt must disappear from my credit reports.”
items.text: Limitation law is about whether a court case can be started, and it differs by province. Credit-report time limits follow separate rules. When a limitation period ends, the debt and the report entry do not always go away.

blocks.text: FCAC: Debt collection—know your rights

sections.title: Build Better Evidence After the Collection

blocks.text: Settling a collection closes one problem. What gets reported next is how you rebuild.
Keep your routine simple enough to repeat.

items.title: Protect every due date
items.text: Pay at least the minimum on time. If a payment looks hard, tell the lender early.

items.title: Lower revolving balances
items.text: Use a small part of your limit and pay the statement balance in full when you can. Do not borrow just to look active.

items.title: Limit applications
items.text: Apply only for credit that solves a real need, and compare the total cost first. Several rushed applications can add hard inquiries.

items.title: Check the reporting
items.text: Give the reports normal time to update, then review both. Dispute wrong balances, dates, owners or statuses with proof.

items.title: Keep the recovery file
items.text: Store the agreement, receipts, letters and corrected reports. Hide account numbers before you share any of it.

items.title: Review at 30, 60 and 90 days
items.text: Track due dates, reported balances, disputes and application results. Look for steady habits, not a set score.

blocks.text: Recent on-time payments and balances you can manage create new evidence. Recovery is a pattern in your reports, not something you buy once.

items.title: “The fastest way to rebuild is to open several credit-building products at once.”
items.text: More accounts can mean more fees, more inquiries and more due dates. One account you can manage may be enough to show recent good habits.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: A collector calls about an account you do not know. What is the first useful move?
items.detail: Collect facts. Confirm the collector, the original creditor, the balance and the written notice before you agree to pay.

items.title: The only way to pay a valid balance is to miss rent. What should guide your plan?
items.detail: Your real cash flow. Choose written terms that protect your essentials and do not need new high-interest borrowing.

items.title: The collector promises on the phone that the entry will be deleted. What do you do?
items.detail: Do not rely on it. Ask for written terms, and remember that settling a debt does not promise that true history is deleted.

items.title: A paid balance still shows as unpaid after normal update time. What goes in your dispute?
items.detail: The agreement, the receipt, the final confirmation and a copy of the wrong report entry.

items.title: Which rebuilding habit comes first?
items.detail: Protect every due date by paying on time.

sections.title: Your Action: Fillable Collections Recovery Record

blocks.text: Use copies of your records. Do not write full account numbers, passwords, PINs, SINs or ID numbers in this workbook.
If your plan cannot survive an ordinary grocery week, it is not a workable plan yet. Adjust the schedule before you commit to it.
Rebuilding after a collection is a set of steps, done in order.
blocks.detail: Check the claim, dispute what is wrong, settle the valid amount on written terms, confirm the reporting and build recent good habits. You are not trying to make the past invisible. You are making the present accurate, so the next decision is easier to support.

items.title: Collection account
items.text: A debt that was handed to a collector after it was not paid as agreed.

items.title: Original creditor
items.text: The business or lender that the account was first owed to.

items.title: Collection agency
items.text: A business that collects debts for a creditor or a debt owner, under the law.

items.title: Settlement
items.text: An agreement to close a debt for an amount the creditor accepts, sometimes less than the claimed balance.

items.title: Reporting period
items.text: How long information can stay on a credit report under the rules and practices that apply.

items.title: Limitation period
items.text: A time limit, set by province, on starting certain court cases. It is not a rule for deleting credit-report entries.

items.title: Recovery file
items.text: A dated set of notices, statements, call logs, agreements, receipts and report copies.
